Latest release · Earlier releases · Next, at the earliest · Or a week later · Window, for irregular pollsters · A slot no release kept

Projections read each pollster’s last eight gaps between releases: they mark the earliest a poll could land, not the likeliest. A pollster that misses its slot shows as overdue for two days, then the forecast moves on to the next plausible date — the × marks where it stood.

Release calendar

The table’s own projections two months out: a date is the earliest that house’s wave could land; a span is a window the wave can fall anywhere in, from a house that keeps no set day. Both come from each house’s recent rhythm, never from a promise — a house that misses its slot stays listed until its wave is added. The Mood of the Nation and Issues Monitor rows (SEC Newgate, Ipsos) publish no vote polls; they are the releases the Direction and issues panels read.

One Nation is gaining more slowly in Tasmania, the ACT and the NT

Since July 2025, the composition of One Nation’s vote has shifted away from Tasmania, the ACT and the NT (−11 points relative to all One Nation voters). Measured from the polls at the election, it has gained ground among over-55s (+5.3 points relative to all voters) and it has gained ground among retirees (+7 points relative to all voters).

Economic sentimentConfidence indices, 100 = neutral, five published series

Confidence is underwater on both counts.

Consumers at 66.2, down 1.7 on the week. Consumers on Westpac–MI’s read at 80.4, down 4 on the month, not far off its low of 80.1 in Apr 2026. Consumers on DemosAU’s index at 38.7, not far off its low of 38.7 in Nov 2026. Businesses at 76.5, down 2.6 on the month, not far off its low of 76.0 in Aug 2026. Businesses on NAB’s survey at −13, down 4 on the month (conditions −1).

How to read this chart

Five published gauges of economic confidence, split into two views — the consumer lanes and the business pair, switched by the tabs over the chart — and set out as each house prints them from the 2025 election on: the weekly ANZ–Roy Morgan consumer index and monthly business index, Westpac–MI’s monthly consumer sentiment and DemosAU’s national consumer-sentiment index, and NAB’s Monthly Business Survey. Each dot is one release, as printed; each line is the same readings smoothed with a recency-weighted kernel (half-life 14 days on the weekly index, 60 days on the monthly ones), so release-to-release noise reads as trend — the quoted figures stay the raw prints. There is no combining across houses and no adjustment for lean — a record, not an estimate.

Behind the current term, the band pools that view’s main gauge over past terms — each term lined up on its own election month, so the bottom axis (months since this term’s election) is every term’s ruler: the middle half of past terms in the heavier fill, the middle 80% in the lighter, their average the dashed line, paler where fewer terms ran that long. Consumer history runs to 1974, business to 2013. “Draw a past term” lifts any single term out of the band as its own smoothed, dotted line in the house’s own colour — and on the consumer view Westpac–MI’s reading of the same term draws beside it, dotted gold where its 1974 series reaches — and “Source data, CSV” in the footer downloads every release and past-term reading. “Show complete history” instead draws whole years: each lane’s own published monthly series runs back as a pale line — ANZ–Roy Morgan’s consumer index to 1973, Westpac–MI’s consumer sentiment to 1974, Roy Morgan’s business index to 2010 — with the releases and their smoothing re-drawn over the file. Westpac–MI months before 2010 come from the OECD’s republication of the index, which rounds them to the nearest whole index point; from 2010 the RBA’s table carries Westpac–MI’s own decimals. NAB stays out of that underlay: its long series is a deviation from its own average, a different measure to its printed net balance, so the NAB lane only ever carries NAB’s own releases.

ANZ–Roy Morgan’s and Westpac–MI’s are indices where 100 is neutral; DemosAU’s national index is 50-neutral and draws doubled to share the line. NAB instead reports a net balance — the share of optimistic firms minus pessimistic ones — where 0 is neutral, so the NAB line is drawn 100 points up to share the neutral line on the business view; the figure beside it and in its tooltips is NAB’s own printed number, and the row also carries the survey’s conditions reading.

The Inflation & growth tab charts the ABS’s and OECD’s official figures exactly as published: Australia’s headline inflation (the ABS’s monthly all-items CPI as an annual change; before the monthly CPI era, the quarterly series derived from the ABS’s own published index numbers, spliced where the printed monthly measure begins), its own deviation from the Reserve Bank’s 2–3% band at its midpoint, real GDP per person and real net national disposable income per person (annual change in chain-volume levels, seasonally adjusted), beside the OECD-wide average and, drawn as dashed context lines, the OECD countries’ own median and the median deviation from each member’s own central-bank target (band targets read at their midpoints; a country joins the median only once both its print and a formal target exist that month, so the line grows as inflation targeting spread after New Zealand’s 1990 band). The shaded band marks the Reserve Bank’s 2–3% inflation target. Nothing is smoothed, adjusted, combined or estimated — official prints, joined as-is, refreshed daily from the ABS and OECD data APIs (the deviation lines are computed here: Australia’s from the ABS’s own figures, the OECD median from the member countries’ OECD-published prints and, since 2026, from the OECD’s monthly inflation release table — one decimal).

Reading economic sentiment beside the polls is context, not a predictor of the vote. The consumer and business gauges needn’t move together, and two houses asking differently worded questions needn’t agree week to week.

Release calendar

The next editions of the four gauges charted above — ANZ–Roy Morgan’s and Westpac–MI’s consumer series, Roy Morgan’s and NAB’s business series — projected from each series’ own release rhythm, exactly as the Latest-polls calendar projects a pollster. A date is the earliest a release could land, never a promise; a series that misses its slot stays listed in the due lead-in until the release is recorded.

About this page

The modern page in old clothes

Every headline, figure and chart here is the modern front page’s own, read from it each time the site is built and drawn the way a website of about 2000 would have drawn it. Where a modern section switches between views, its panel here offers the same switch.

More in the modern view

The modern page adds tooltips and time ranges to its charts, the primary vote by pollster or group of voters, and each latest poll opened in full. All polls and Past cycles have retro views too, and so does the Electoral map.

auspol tracker is an unofficial aggregator of published federal opinion polling.

Best efforts are made to make the aggregate figures transparent, trustworthy, statistically sound, and informative, but they are, in the end, estimates only.

How the figures are built is in Info. Spot an error, a missing poll, or have any other feedback? Please let me know.

Federal polling archives I’ve located are stored here for safekeeping and convenience.
